summary:
A visitor in the Basque Country stands under the national framework of Spain: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 1 March 2023 as the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, applies uniformly across the autonomous communities, and this region has enacted no separate trans statute of its own. Title II allows adults to rectify the registered sex marker by simple declaration, with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for corresponding adaptation of identity documents.

The law also mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications still pending at entry into force. Human Rights Watch, reporting on the passage by the Congress of Deputies on 16 February 2023, described the self-identification route as a simple administrative process replacing the former requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment, and placed the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate conditions for legal gender recognition.

Ley 4/2023 further expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before they can consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Children from age 12 can obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious during the passage debate.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the Civil Registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Spanish Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. Both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based attack has no free-standing offence to charge; Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. A Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied throughout Spain since 2005. The 2024 national report on LGTBI-motivated offences places this region at the top of the per-capita rates, a figure best read as intensive reporting and counting rather than evidence of danger: the regional government operates its own LGTBI public-order policing and an equality observatory, and no regional statutory rollback exists. Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.
tangentialFactors:
The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions alongside the national framework. The Basque Parliament passed a law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people, dated 2013 in the available source, which for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention within the Basque education system.

Institutional markers predate that statute by decades: the first Basque Pride march took place in Bilbao in 1978, the activist collective EHGAM was legalised in 1983, and Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, was created in 1988. The region's own equality infrastructure is therefore long-standing rather than a response to the 2023 national reform.

Administrative self-declaration places Spain alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in the comparative set used for gender-recognition regimes. Public opinion in the region runs in the same direction: a 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that nine in ten Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex.
localsOnly:
Residents draw on both layers. The 2013 Basque statute on gender identity and trans rights imposes non-discrimination obligations within regional competence, and Emakunde functions as the standing regional equality body for complaints and information.

Osakidetza, the Basque health service, has provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation and reaffirmed that position in 2013. National policy adds publicly mandated health measures under Ley 4/2023, including the ban on medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before consent.

Residents also fall under the national consent rules for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition of gender identity is possible from age 12 under conditions. Applications for rectification that were already pending when Ley 4/2023 entered into force are handled under its transitory provisions.

Parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples and the full adoption rights in force since 2005 are resident-facing entitlements that follow from the national framework rather than from any regional act.
